[0.00 - 4.96] Ever wondered how Google translates an entire webpage to a different language in a matter
[4.96 - 11.12] of seconds? Or your phone gallery group's images based on their location? All of this is a product
[11.12 - 17.20] of deep learning. But what exactly is deep learning? Deep learning is a subset of machine
[17.20 - 22.80] learning, which in turn is a subset of artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is a
[22.80 - 28.24] technique that enables a machine to mimic human behavior. Machine learning is a technique to
[28.32 - 34.56] achieve AI through algorithms trained with data. And finally, deep learning is a type of machine
[34.56 - 40.08] learning inspired by the structure of the human brain. In terms of deep learning, this structure
[40.08 - 45.60] is called an artificial neural network. Let's understand deep learning better and how it's
[45.60 - 50.80] different from machine learning. Say we create a machine that could differentiate between tomatoes
[50.80 - 55.76] and cherries. If done using machine learning, we'd have to tell the machine the features
[55.76 - 61.04] based on which the two can be differentiated. These features could be the size and the type
[61.04 - 66.32] of stem on them. With deep learning on the other hand, the features are picked out by the neural
[66.32 - 71.84] network without human intervention. Of course, that kind of independence comes at the cost of
[71.84 - 77.68] having a much higher volume of data to train our machine. Now, let's dive into the working of
[77.68 - 83.92] neural networks. Here we have three students, each of them write down the digit nine on a piece of
[83.92 - 90.56] paper. Notably, they don't all write it identically. The human brain can easily recognize the digits.
[91.20 - 97.44] But what if a computer had to recognize them? That's where deep learning comes in. Here's a
[97.44 - 103.84] neural network trained to identify handwritten digits. Each number is present as an image of 28
[103.84 - 112.24] times 28 pixels. Now, that amounts to a total of 784 pixels. Neurons, the core entity of a neural
[112.24 - 119.68] network, is where the information processing takes place. Each of the 784 pixels is fed to a neuron
[119.68 - 126.24] in the first layer of our neural network. This forms the input layer. On the other end, we have
[126.24 - 132.32] the output layer with each neuron representing a digit with the hidden layers existing between them.
[132.32 - 138.16] The information is transferred from one layer to another over connecting channels. Each of these
[138.16 - 144.08] has a value attached to it and hence is called a weighted channel. All neurons have a unique
[144.08 - 150.40] number associated with it called bias. This bias is added to the weighted sum of inputs
[150.40 - 156.24] reaching the neuron, which is then applied to a function known as the activation function.
[156.88 - 161.28] The result of the activation function determines if the neuron gets activated.
[161.76 - 168.00] Every activated neuron passes on information to the following layers. This continues up till
[168.00 - 175.44] the second last layer. The one neuron activated in the output layer corresponds to the input digit.
[175.44 - 180.48] The weights and bias are continuously adjusted to produce a well-trained network.
[180.48 - 186.16] So, where is deep learning applied? In customer support, when most people converse with customer
[186.16 - 192.00] support agents, the conversation seems so real. They don't even realize that it's actually a
[192.00 - 198.32] bot on the other side. In medical care, neural networks detect cancer cells and analyze MRI
[198.32 - 205.52] images to give detailed results. Self-driving cars. What seemed like science fiction is now
[205.52 - 212.16] a reality. Apple, Tesla, and Nissan are only a few of the companies working on self-driving cars,
[212.16 - 217.84] so deep learning has a vast scope, but it too faces some limitations.
[217.84 - 223.12] The first as we discussed earlier is data. While deep learning is the most efficient
[223.12 - 229.20] way to deal with unstructured data, a neural network requires a massive volume of data to train.
[229.20 - 234.16] Let's assume we always have access to the necessary amount of data. Processing this
[234.16 - 240.48] is not within the capability of every machine, and that brings us to our second limitation,
[240.56 - 246.56] computational power. Training a neural network requires graphical processing units,
[246.56 - 253.92] which have thousands of cores as compared to CPUs, and GPUs are of course more expensive.
[253.92 - 261.28] And finally, we come down to training time. Deep neural networks take hours or even months to train.
[261.28 - 266.24] The time increases with the amount of data and number of layers in the network.
